name: Acerola fruit extract
lead: Acerola fruit extract is a preparation made from the fruit of Malpighia emarginata, a tropical shrub native to the Lesser Antilles and northern South America and grown commercially in Brazil and other warm regions. The raw fruit is among the richest natural sources of vitamin C, with one nutrition table listing roughly 1,678 mg per 100 g.[1]

In skincare and beauty nutrition, acerola extract appears mainly as a natural vitamin C source in drinkable and oral supplements, often alongside collagen peptides, zinc, biotin and vitamin E. The appearance rationale is a chain: vitamin C is a cofactor for the enzymes that stabilise collagen, and collagen supports skin firmness.[5] It is also used in the food industry, for example as a natural antioxidant in meat products.[2][3]

Evidence for an appearance effect specific to acerola is limited. A randomized, placebo-controlled study tested a multi-ingredient drink that contained acerola extract together with collagen peptides and other nutrients in women aged 35 and older, but because the product was a blend, the contribution of acerola alone cannot be separated.[2]

paras: Acerola is a fruit-bearing shrub or small tree of the family Malpighiaceae. Its fruit is highly perishable, lasting only a few days at ambient temperature, which is one reason it is commonly processed into juice, concentrates and powders.[1] Vitamin C content is highest in unripe fruit and declines as the fruit ripens, and immature green fruit is harvested for industrial vitamin C production.[1]

Acerola is also called Barbados cherry, West Indian cherry and Puerto Rican cherry; the name derives from an Arabic term for the azarole, an Old World fruit of similar appearance.[1] It is native to the Lesser Antilles and extends into South America as far as Brazil, and has naturalized in Peru, Venezuela, Ecuador, southern Florida and the Lower Rio Grande Valley of Texas.[1] The evergreen shrub fruits within its first year, with yields peaking around the sixth year at up to 47 kg per plant, and the fruit is picked frequently because it does not store well on the tree.[1] Brazil is the largest producer, growing it on about 11,000 hectares for roughly 33,000 tonnes annually, and a university in Pernambuco established a germplasm bank in 1998 to preserve the crop's genetic diversity.[1]

Vitamin C is a cofactor for the enzymes that hydroxylate proline and lysine, which allows collagen to assume its triple-helix structure; collagen made without enough vitamin C is unstable, and scurvy is the disease of deficiency.[5] The US recommended dietary allowance is 90 mg per day for adult men and 75 mg for adult women, with a tolerable upper intake level of 2,000 mg, and the article notes that fruits and vegetables are the richest natural sources and that absorption efficiency falls at large supplement doses.[5] Large doses may cause stomach discomfort, headache, sleep problems and flushing.[5]
Supplement makers cite this biochemistry when including acerola, but the skin trial involving acerola tested a blend, so the share of any effect due to acerola's vitamin C cannot be separated.[2]

Acerola extract is marketed as a plant-derived vitamin C source in beauty-from-within supplements aimed at skin firmness, hydration and photoprotection. The best-known published example is a drinking ampoule containing 2.5 g of collagen peptides plus acerola extract, vitamin C, zinc, biotin and a vitamin E complex.[2]

Acerola is eaten raw, juiced and used in jams, concentrates and liqueurs. Acerola powder is used as a bread improver in some commercial breads, and its pigments have been suggested as food colorants.[1] A 2015 meat-science study evaluated acerola extract as an antioxidant additive in beef patties, assessing sensory quality and shelf life.[3]

One randomized, placebo-controlled, blind study enrolled 72 healthy women aged 35 or older (36 per group) to take a drinkable nutraceutical for skin aging; the product combined collagen peptides, acerola extract, vitamin C, zinc, biotin and vitamin E, and outcomes included skin hydration, elasticity, roughness and density.[2] Because every ingredient was given together, the study does not isolate acerola. Reported measurements in that study covered skin hydration, elasticity, roughness and density over the intervention period, and the authors concluded the blend improved skin aging parameters compared with placebo.[2]

A registered trial on an 8-week dietary supplement and minimal erythema dose (sunburn threshold) has been listed on ClinicalTrials.gov; the registry entry does not identify acerola as a sole ingredient.[4] No trial of acerola extract alone for skin appearance was found.
The fruit itself is a food. The leaves and leaf stalks bear minute stinging hairs that can irritate skin.[1] No safety signal specific to acerola extract in cosmetic use is documented.

Acerola powder is used as a bread improver in some commercial breads, and its pigments have been proposed as natural food colorants.[1] No looksmaxxing community protocols specific to acerola were found; it appears mainly as an ingredient in beauty and antioxidant supplement blends.

lore.intro: Acerola is discussed rarely on its own; it appears as an ingredient inside antioxidant and beauty-supplement blends.

claims.claim: Natural acerola vitamin C is a better skin supplement than synthetic ascorbic acid
claims.believers: Supplement marketing presents acerola as a whole-fruit, plant-derived vitamin C source.
claims.experts: No published trial compares acerola extract with ascorbic acid for skin appearance; the one skin study tested a multi-ingredient blend.[2]

claims.claim: Drinking vitamin C blends firms the skin
claims.believers: Beauty-from-within products cite vitamin C's role in collagen formation alongside collagen peptides.[5]
claims.experts: A randomized placebo-controlled trial of 72 women found improvements with a blend including collagen peptides and acerola, but it cannot attribute effects to acerola alone.[2]

card.summary: Vitamin-C-rich tropical fruit extract used in beauty supplements; skin evidence exists only for multi-ingredient blends.
card.note: Published skin data come from a blended product, not acerola alone.

quick.overview:
Acerola extract comes from a tropical fruit that is one of the richest natural sources of vitamin C. It is added to oral beauty supplements and drinks as a plant-based vitamin C source.
The one controlled skin study found tested a multi-ingredient drink, so effects specific to acerola have not been separated out.
quick.mechanism: Vitamin C is a cofactor in collagen synthesis and an antioxidant; acerola is used to supply it in a natural-sounding form.
quick.risks: The fruit is a food and no cosmetic-specific safety concerns are documented. The plant's leaves have stinging hairs that can irritate skin.

chain: Vitamin C is a cofactor in collagen formation
Proponents expect firmer, better-hydrated skin when taken with collagen and other nutrients
angle.text: Acerola extract is taken in drinks and capsules as a natural vitamin C source for 'beauty from within' routines aimed at skin firmness and hydration. The published skin trial used a multi-ingredient blend.
